sections.title: SECTION B: Intern Mental Health Providers
sections.bodyHtml:
This section applies to individuals participating in Inner Strength Institute’s Student Training Program as practicum students, interns, or trainees enrolled in an approved academic program. Intern Mental Health Providers function in a training capacity and do not hold independent clinical authority or employee status unless expressly stated in a written agreement.

Interns provide services solely for educational and training purposes under close supervision and within strict scope-of-practice limitations defined by the Practice, the academic institution, and applicable law.

Role Definition and Educational Purpose

The Intern Mental Health Provider role exists to support the student’s academic and professional development through supervised, hands-on clinical experience. Internship placements are designed to meet educational requirements while maintaining client safety, ethical practice, and compliance with regulatory and payer standards.

Intern participation does not guarantee employment, future role placement, or advancement within the Practice.

Scope of Practice and Authorized Activities

When authorized by the Practice and academic institution, Intern Mental Health Providers may:

  • Observe, assist, co-facilitate, and conduct counseling sessions under supervision
  • Participate in intake processes and assist with gathering clinical information
  • Support the development and implementation of treatment or service plans in collaboration with supervising clinicians
  • Apply evidence-informed, developmentally appropriate interventions consistent with training level
  • Facilitate or support client group sessions only within the approved training and supervision plan and the written authorization required by Group counseling authorization
  • Provide services in approved ISI office and telehealth settings as assigned

All services must be approved in advance, supervised, and aligned with the intern’s training level and educational objectives.

Prohibited Activities and Clinical Limitations

Intern Mental Health Providers may not:

  • Practice independently or without supervision
  • Independently develop, modify, or terminate treatment plans or diagnose mental disorders without the approval of a Licensed Clinical Supervisor.
  • Represent themselves as licensed or independently credentialed providers
  • Provide services outside approved programs, supervision, or training agreements
  • Bill services independently or assume billing authority

Interns must not exceed the scope authorized by the Practice or academic institution, regardless of prior experience.

Supervision Requirements and Authority

Intern Mental Health Providers are subject to direct clinical supervision at all times.

  • Supervisors are designated by the Practice
  • Supervisors retain full clinical responsibility for services provided by interns
  • Supervisors must approve services, documentation, and clinical decisions
  • Interns must participate in individual supervision, group supervision, case reviews, and training as required

Supervision structure, documentation and tracking follow SUPERVISION PROCEDURES and SUPERVISION AND PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT. Student placements retain their program-specific supervision requirements; the pre-licensed 60/40 benefit milestone does not automatically reduce student supervision.

Documentation Responsibilities

Interns are responsible for completing documentation accurately and timely, consistent with training level and Practice standards.

Documentation:

  • Must be reviewed and co-signed by the designated supervisor
  • Must remain within intern scope and training expectations
  • Must adhere to documentation timelines and correction procedures

Incomplete, late, or inaccurate documentation may impact training status or continuation in the program.

Billing and Compensation

Intern Mental Health Providers do not bill independently.

  • Any billing of intern-provided services occurs under the supervising clinician’s authority
  • Billing eligibility and codes require written Practice and payer authorization, supervision and an applicable training agreement. Employment status and any compensation follow STUDENT CLASSIFICATION and the individual written agreement.
  • Training participation alone does not authorize billing or determine employee status. For students separately engaged as employees, compensable work remains payable under Actual time, support activities and corrections.

Unauthorized billing activity is prohibited.

Professional Conduct and Center-Based Expectations

Interns are expected to maintain professional conduct consistent with Practice policies, academic training standards, and ISI site requirements.

Interns must:

  • Adhere to confidentiality and HIPAA requirements
  • Maintain appropriate boundaries with clients, families, and ISI team members
  • Follow escalation and safety protocols
  • Represent the Practice professionally in all settings

Relationship to Other Handbook Sections

This section must be read in conjunction with:

  • Student Training Program
  • Supervision and Training
  • Workplace Policies and Standards
  • Role Descriptions and Typical Duties (when applicable)
  • Program-Specific Sections

Where conflicts arise, educational purpose and supervision authority prevail.

Section B Summary

Intern Mental Health Providers participate in structured, supervised training experiences that prioritize learning, ethical practice, and client safety. This section defines the boundaries and expectations of intern roles to prevent scope drift, ensure compliance, and support high-quality training outcomes.

sections.title: SECTION C: Pre-Licensed and Unlicensed Master’s-Level Providers (Tier 2)
sections.bodyHtml:
This section applies to employees who hold a Master’s degree in a mental health–related field and are functioning in roles that require advanced clinical knowledge but do not confer independent licensure authority. This includes pre-licensed clinicians actively pursuing licensure and unlicensed Master’s-level providers practicing in roles where licensure is not required or not applicable.

Tier 2 providers deliver clinical and therapeutic services under defined supervision requirements and within Practice-approved scope. Authorization to provide or bill services is determined by credentialing status, supervision, payer requirements, and program approval—not solely by degree attainment or licensure intent.

Role Definition and Professional Standing

Pre-Licensed and Unlicensed Master’s-Level Providers occupy an intermediate role between training positions and fully licensed clinical practice. These providers are qualified to deliver therapeutic services consistent with their education and training but remain subject to ongoing oversight, supervision, and Practice authorization.

Licensure pursuit may be required, optional, or not applicable depending on role designation, program assignment, and funding source. Regardless of licensure intent, Tier 2 providers do not practice independently.

Scope of Practice and Authorized Clinical Activities

When authorized by the Practice, Tier 2 providers may:

  • Provide authorized individual and family-based therapeutic services aligned with approved treatment or service plans. Client group delivery also requires the written authorization in Group counseling authorization
  • Conduct clinical assessments and contribute to diagnostic impressions under supervision
  • Develop, implement, and update treatment plans subject to supervisory review
  • Utilize evidence-based and developmentally appropriate clinical interventions consistent with training and supervision
  • Collaborate with families and interdisciplinary teams as permitted by consent
  • Provide services in approved ISI office and telehealth settings as assigned

Tier 2 providers may exercise clinical judgment within their authorized scope, subject to supervision and escalation requirements.

Clinical Authority Limits and Prohibited Activities

Pre-Licensed and Unlicensed Master’s-Level Providers may not:

  • Practice independently or without required supervision
  • Represent themselves as fully licensed clinicians
  • Provide services outside approved credentialing, payer, or program authorization
  • Ignore or override supervisory direction
  • Assume authority for high-risk clinical decisions without consultation

Independent practice authority is not granted until full licensure and Practice approval are obtained.

Supervision Requirements and Milestones

Tier 2 providers are subject to structured clinical supervision.

  • Supervision frequency, format, and documentation are determined by licensure status, payer rules, and Practice policy
  • Supervisors retain oversight authority and may review, co-sign, or redirect clinical work
  • Providers must escalate safety concerns, ethical dilemmas, scope questions, or complex cases

For pre-licensed providers, supervision may also count toward licensure requirements when conducted by an approved supervisor. Milestone transitions (e.g., increased autonomy, expanded caseloads) are not automatic and require documented approval. For the pre-licensed benefit transition, use the confirmed 60 completed individual/triadic hours plus 40 group opportunities offered in SUPERVISION PROCEDURES. Offered opportunities are not completed licensure hours, and this milestone does not create independent practice authority.

Documentation Responsibilities

Tier 2 providers are responsible for timely, accurate, and clinically appropriate documentation.

Documentation must:

  • Support medical necessity and clinical rationale
  • Accurately reflect services provided and interventions used
  • Align with treatment plans and service authorization
  • Comply with payer, regulatory, and Practice standards

Documentation may be subject to supervisory review, audit, and correction.

Billing and Service Authorization

Pre-Licensed and Unlicensed Master’s-Level Providers may bill services only when authorized by the Practice and permitted by payer and program rules.

  • Billing eligibility depends on credentialing, supervision, and payer requirements
  • Providers must confirm authorization prior to service delivery
  • Billing execution, code authorization and compensation follow Service-code compensation and authorizations, the individual employment agreement and Actual time, support activities and corrections.

Unauthorized or non-compliant billing may result in corrective action.

Center-Based and Interdisciplinary Practice

When practicing in center-based or interdisciplinary environments, Tier 2 providers must:

  • Maintain professional boundaries and role clarity
  • Coordinate appropriately with ISI personnel while adhering to confidentiality requirements
  • Follow escalation, safety, and crisis protocols
  • Represent the Practice professionally and within scope

Program placement does not expand or alter clinical authority.

Relationship to Other Handbook Sections

This section must be read in conjunction with:

  • Supervision and Training
  • Career Pathways and Compensation
  • Service-code compensation and authorizations
  • Role Descriptions and Typical Duties
  • Program-Specific Sections

Where conflicts arise, supervision requirements and payer authorization prevail.

Section C Summary

Pre-Licensed and Unlicensed Master’s-Level Providers deliver advanced clinical services under supervision while progressing toward greater professional responsibility. This section establishes clear authority limits, supervision expectations, and billing boundaries to ensure ethical practice, regulatory compliance, and client safety.

sections.title: SECTION D: Licensed Providers and Clinical Supervisors (Tier 3)
sections.bodyHtml:
This section applies to employees holding an active, unrestricted clinical license recognized by the Practice, including Licensed Professional Counselors (LPC), Licensed Marriage and Family Therapists (LMFT), Licensed Clinical Social Workers (LCSW), and other licensed clinicians authorized by Inner Strength Institute to provide independent clinical services.

Licensed Providers may also hold Clinical Supervisor designations when approved by the Practice. Tier 3 providers are entrusted with the highest level of clinical authority, accountability, and professional responsibility within the organization.

Role Definition and Professional Authority

Licensed Providers are authorized to practice independently within the scope of their license and Practice approval. This includes full responsibility for clinical decision-making, treatment planning, risk assessment, and therapeutic intervention.

Licensed Providers serve as the clinical backbone of the Practice, supporting client care, supervising less-credentialed staff when designated, and upholding ethical, legal, and professional standards across programs and settings.

Scope of Practice and Authorized Clinical Activities

When credentialed and authorized by the Practice, Licensed Providers may:

  • Provide authorized individual, family and collateral psychotherapy. Client group psychotherapy requires existing written authorization or an express written exception under Group counseling authorization
  • Conduct clinical assessments, establish diagnoses, and determine medical necessity
  • Develop, modify, and terminate treatment plans independently
  • Select and implement evidence-based clinical interventions within licensure scope
  • Provide crisis assessment, intervention, and stabilization
  • Collaborate with interdisciplinary teams and external providers
  • Deliver services in approved ISI office and telehealth settings
  • Participate in program development, consultation, and leadership activities

Licensed Providers are responsible for ensuring all services align with licensure requirements, payer rules, and Practice standards.

Clinical Judgment, Risk, and Crisis Authority

Licensed Providers retain primary authority and responsibility for:

  • Risk assessment and safety planning
  • Determination of clinical urgency and escalation
  • Crisis intervention and post-crisis follow-up
  • Mandatory reporting decisions
  • Ethical decision-making and professional boundaries

When supervising others, Licensed Providers must actively monitor risk, intervene as needed, and ensure appropriate documentation and follow-up.

Supervision Responsibilities and Oversight Authority

Licensed Providers approved as Clinical Supervisors hold formal oversight responsibility for supervisees.

Supervisory responsibilities may include:

  • Clinical oversight and guidance
  • Review and co-signing of documentation
  • Ensuring supervisee compliance with scope, ethics, and payer rules
  • Providing feedback, education, and corrective guidance
  • Escalating concerns related to safety, performance, or compliance

Supervisors retain shared accountability for services provided under their supervision. Failure to supervise appropriately may result in corrective action or removal of supervisory designation.

The structure and mechanics of supervision follow SUPERVISION PROCEDURES. Direct supervision is paid at 100% of the individually contracted supervision hourly rate, group hosting at 150%, and actual review/co-signing of another provider’s notes at 50%, under Actual time, support activities and corrections. Clinical oversight duties and pay for actual work remain separate from payer reimbursement.

Documentation and Accountability

Licensed Providers are responsible for ensuring that documentation:

  • Accurately reflects services provided
  • Supports diagnosis, medical necessity, and treatment rationale
  • Meets payer, regulatory, and Practice standards
  • Is completed timely and accurately

When supervising others, Licensed Providers are responsible for reviewing documentation and addressing deficiencies. Repeated documentation issues may trigger audits or corrective action.

Billing and Compliance Responsibility

Licensed Providers may bill services in accordance with credentialing status, payer rules, and Practice authorization.

Licensed Providers must:

  • Ensure services billed are appropriate, authorized, and compliant
  • Avoid misrepresentation of services or credentials
  • Oversee billing activity for supervised staff when applicable

Billing execution and coding rules follow Service-code compensation and authorizations and applicable billing policies. Client group services require express written approval for group counseling under Group counseling authorization. Obtain approval before advertising, enrolling or scheduling; a role, credential or saved code mapping does not authorize group delivery.

Ethical Leadership and Professional Conduct

Licensed Providers are expected to model ethical conduct, professionalism, and clinical integrity across all settings.

This includes:

  • Adherence to licensure board ethics and legal requirements
  • Maintenance of professional boundaries
  • Appropriate use of authority and influence
  • Respectful collaboration with staff, clients, and partners
  • Avoidance of role confusion or scope drift

Licensed Providers are expected to uphold Practice values and serve as professional leaders within the organization.

Relationship to Other Handbook Sections

This section must be read in conjunction with:

  • Supervision and Training
  • Legal and Ethical Compliance
  • Career Pathways and Compensation
  • Service-code compensation and authorizations
  • Program-Specific Sections

Where conflicts arise, licensure requirements, payer rules, and supervisory responsibility prevail.

Section D Summary

Licensed Providers and Clinical Supervisors hold the highest level of clinical authority and accountability within the Practice. This section establishes independent practice authority while clearly defining supervisory responsibility, ethical leadership expectations, and compliance obligations to protect clients, staff, and the organization.

sections.title: SECTION E: Non-Clinical Staff
sections.bodyHtml:
This section applies to employees and contractors whose roles are administrative, operational, managerial, technical, or support-based and who do not provide clinical or therapeutic services. This includes, but is not limited to administrative staff, operations personnel, coordinators, billing and support staff, outreach staff, and management roles that do not involve clinical service delivery.

Non-Clinical Staff play a vital role in supporting the Practice’s mission by ensuring organizational stability, compliance, coordination, and effective service delivery infrastructure. These roles do not carry clinical authority.

Role Definition and Purpose

Non-Clinical Staff support the Practice through operational and administrative duties such as coordination, communication, billing, scheduling, technology and program support. These duties support client access and continuity of care but do not involve diagnosis, treatment or clinical decision-making. Required meetings, onboarding, training and assigned internal work follow 14. Support Activity and Actual time, support activities and corrections. Use the applicable salary agreement or individual duty rate; an administrative job title does not automatically classify all work as Indirect Service.

Non-Clinical Staff must maintain clear boundaries between operational support and clinical care at all times.

Scope of Responsibilities

When authorized by role and assignment, Non-Clinical Staff may:

  • Perform administrative, operational, scheduling, billing, or coordination tasks
  • Support program logistics, onboarding, data entry, record management, or reporting
  • Communicate with families or partners regarding scheduling, logistics, or non-clinical matters
  • Support staff through coordination, information sharing, and systems management
  • Participate in organizational meetings, trainings, and professional development as required

Non-Clinical Staff must operate strictly within the scope of their assigned duties.

Prohibited Activities and Clinical Boundaries

Non-Clinical Staff may not:

  • Provide clinical services, counseling, or therapeutic interventions
  • Diagnose mental health conditions or make clinical recommendations
  • Interpret clinical information for clients or families
  • Provide guidance that could be construed as clinical advice
  • Represent themselves as clinicians or clinical authorities
  • Engage in documentation intended to serve as clinical records

Any situation involving clinical questions, treatment decisions, or client risk must be escalated to an appropriate clinical provider or supervisor.

Confidentiality and Information Access

Non-Clinical Staff may access client or employee information only as necessary to perform assigned duties and must adhere to all confidentiality, privacy, and HIPAA requirements.

  • Access to clinical records is role-limited and purpose-specific
  • Information obtained through administrative access may not be shared outside authorized channels
  • Confidentiality obligations continue following separation from employment

Improper access, use, or disclosure of information may result in corrective action.

Center-Based and Client-Adjacent Conduct

When Non-Clinical Staff are present in ISI service or client-adjacent environments, they must:

  • Adhere to ISI site professionalism, safety, and conduct standards
  • Maintain appropriate boundaries with students, families, and ISI personnel
  • Avoid involvement in client-specific discussions beyond logistical coordination
  • Refer all clinical questions or concerns to designated clinical staff

Presence in an ISI service or program setting does not authorize clinical engagement.

Communication and Representation

Non-Clinical Staff must represent the Practice accurately and professionally in all communications.

  • Communication with clients or families should remain logistical and informational
  • Clinical questions must be redirected to authorized providers
  • Staff must avoid language that implies clinical judgment, diagnosis, or treatment

All external communications must align with Practice policies and role authorization. Use the app records and secure communication procedures in App records, forms and timekeeping.

Supervision, Accountability, and Escalation

Non-Clinical Staff are accountable to their designated supervisor or manager.

  • Concerns related to safety, ethics, compliance, or boundary issues must be escalated promptly
  • Non-Clinical Staff must seek guidance when uncertain about role boundaries
  • Failure to maintain boundaries or comply with Practice policies may result in corrective action

Relationship to Other Handbook Sections

This section must be read in conjunction with:

  • Workplace Policies and Standards
  • Confidentiality and Privacy
  • Performance and Expectations

Where conflicts arise, non-clinical role limitations prevail.

Section E Summary

Non-Clinical Staff support the Practice through essential administrative and operational functions while maintaining clear boundaries from clinical service delivery. This section establishes expectations that protect clients, staff, and the organization by preventing role confusion and ensuring appropriate escalation of clinical matters.

sections.title: PROGRAM OVERVIEW
sections.bodyHtml:
The Student Training Program at our Practice offers a dynamic and multifaceted learning experience for students embarking on their professional journey in our field. This program encompasses both a practicum phase for those beginning their practical training and an internship phase for students who are ready to engage in a more advanced, hands-on experience. Students may enter the program at either stage, depending on their educational needs and previous experience, ensuring a tailored approach to their professional development.

Clinical counseling placement

ISI uses the shared Student Training Program for clinical counseling practicum and internship placements. Placements occur in approved offices or approved telehealth settings. The training plan identifies permitted clinical duties, learning objectives, required supervision and the assigned clinical supervisor.

Placement records, the training agreement, supervision, actual-time records and evaluations are maintained in the app. The Clinical Development Supervision Rubric is the actual quarterly evaluation form. Clinical authority depends on the approved training plan, credentials, supervision and applicable payer requirements.

sections.title: Student Training Agreement and Placement Plan
sections.bodyHtml:
The student, assigned supervisor and authorized practice representative complete the placement agreement in the app before clinical placement begins. The agreement identifies the student’s academic program, practicum or internship phase, start and end dates, approved service setting, learning objectives, permitted duties, assigned supervisor, supervision schedule and required academic coordination.

Record the applicable student or employee classification, any compensation agreement, confidentiality obligations, required orientation, emergency procedures and acknowledgment of the Student Training Program. Record changes to the placement plan in the app so the current responsibilities and supervision are identifiable.

Use Student supervision and professional development for required supervision, Insurance and liability coverage for practice-provided coverage, and Appendix G: student training evaluation for quarterly assessment. Keep signed agreements and individual evaluations private; the handbook shows the policy and blank form.

The agreement does not waive wage protections or expand a student’s clinical scope. Clinical services must remain authorized and supervised throughout the placement.

sections.title: PROGRAM STRUCTURE
sections.bodyHtml:
Phases of Engagement

Practicum Phase:

For students starting their practical training, this phase focuses on foundational learning and skill development within a structured, supervised environment.

Internship Phase:

Designed for students who have either completed the practicum phase or possess equivalent experience, this phase offers an opportunity for deeper immersion into practical work, allowing students to refine their skills and knowledge in a real-world setting.

Placement Status

Students are engaged as part of our team, either as practicum students or interns, for a specific period. The program begins effectively on a predetermined Commencement Date, with the possibility of transitioning between phases based on successful completion and mutual agreement. Participation is a training placement; any separate employee engagement must be documented under STUDENT CLASSIFICATION.

Ending the Placement

Either the student or the Practice may end the training agreement under its terms. A separate employee engagement is governed by its written employment agreement and the applicable employee policies; placement participation alone does not create employee status.

Location and Scope

Student placements occur at approved ISI offices and through approved virtual services under the training plan and required supervision. Assignments are limited to counseling and the supervised clinical and administrative work that supports the placement.

Focus on Education and Training:

Regardless of the phase, the primary purpose of the program is educational. Whether students are engaged in billable services or other professional activities, the emphasis remains on learning, skill development, and professional growth.

sections.title: EXPECTATIONS OF STUDENT
sections.bodyHtml:
Duties and Professional Conduct:

Students are required to perform duties under Practice supervision, focusing on educational and professional development objectives. This includes adhering to ethical standards and professional conduct as required by regulatory and accrediting authorities.

Participation in Services:

Students' involvement in billable services is subject to Practice evaluation, ensuring alignment with educational goals. Written role, payer and program authorization remain required under Service-code compensation and authorizations. Client group services require express written approval for group counseling under Group counseling authorization. Obtain approval before advertising, enrolling or scheduling; a role, credential or saved code mapping does not authorize group delivery.

Documentation and Reporting:

Complete session notes SHOULD be completed and submitted within 24 hours of each session.

Completed session notes MUST be submitted by Sunday night at 11:59pm of the week for which the session occurred.

Notes completed outside of this timeframe are considered Late and Deficient. Documentation deficiencies may affect training review and must be corrected. For students separately engaged as employees, a late note does not erase pay for compensable work; follow Actual time, support activities and corrections.

Feedback and Compliance:

Students are expected to discuss concerns with their supervisor and comply with all Practice regulations and instructions, including those governing work conditions and legal ordinances.

Specific Duties:

These include, but are not limited to, observing and conducting counseling sessions, participating in intake assessments, completing administrative tasks, maintaining client confidentiality, and engaging in outreach activities. Duties must remain within the approved training plan and role scope. Client group work requires the written authorization in Group counseling authorization.

sections.title: SUPERVISION AND PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT
sections.bodyHtml:
Mentorship:

Each student is paired with a mentor, titled “Clinical Practice Assistant,” for, at minimum, biweekly sessions and initial orientation. Mentors provide guidance across various aspects of the program, including additional educational activities.

Supervision:

Regular supervision sessions, at least once weekly, are conducted with an assigned supervisor. These sessions are critical for feedback, performance evaluation, and aligning with educational objectives. This student-program requirement is separate from the pre-licensed 60/40 benefit transition. Use SUPERVISION PROCEDURES for authorized platforms, reviewed summaries and documentation; separately employed students’ compensable work follows Actual time, support activities and corrections.

sections.title: DISCLOSURE AND LIABILITY
sections.bodyHtml:
Prior Liabilities:

Students are responsible for any liability related to their practicum or employment before joining the Practice.

Insurance and Liability Coverage:

The Practice provides liability insurance and clinical malpractice insurance for its authorized operations, including authorized clinical work performed by employees and clinical students/interns. Coverage is subject to the applicable insurance policy terms and the individual’s authorized role and supervision. This handbook does not extend coverage to unrelated outside activities or promise coverage for work performed before joining the Practice. Request a certificate of insurance or clarification of coverage from People Operations through the app.

sections.bodyHtml: Practicum students and interns participate as trainees under the applicable training or affiliation agreement. A training placement does not automatically make a student an employee or a 1099 contractor. Where a student also holds an employee role, the individual employment agreement and applicable employee compensation, timekeeping, leave and benefit policies govern that work. Training purpose does not remove protections applicable to an employee.

sections.title: Spanish-language intake and handoff
sections.bodyHtml:
Record the client’s and parent/guardian’s primary languages separately in the app’s intake record and client profile. When a parent or guardian prefers Spanish, arrange a Spanish-speaking parent intake through the agency’s Spanish intake team.

  1. Request availability: Open Messages by Conversa and choose the Spanish / Español group. Request a parent-intake time without posting identifying clinical information to the group.
  2. Assign the Spanish-speaking provider: Support coordinates the handoff and adds that provider to the individual client’s authorized care team. Group membership alone does not grant access to client records.
  3. Complete the intake: The Spanish-speaking provider conducts the parent intake and completes its documentation in the client record. The primary provider may attend if helpful.
  4. Prepare the care summary: The primary provider uses the Note Aid treatment-summary workflow to prepare a brief, relevant summary, reviews it for accuracy, and saves the reviewed summary in the authorized medical record. The assigned Spanish-speaking provider accesses it there.
  5. Continue coordination: The assigned Spanish-speaking provider handles future parent check-ins and coordination of care, documenting contacts and sharing relevant updates with the primary provider through the client record.
  6. When coverage is unavailable: Ask support to arrange appropriate language assistance. Do not use children as interpreters or treat an unsuccessful English-language contact as a refusal of services.

In your Provider Update, list languages you can use proficiently enough to conduct sessions and select your proficiency. Update support when your availability changes.

sections.title: Clinical Development Supervision Rubric
sections.bodyHtml:
Purpose:

This rubric is used by supervisors to evaluate the clinical performance, development, and professional behaviors of supervisees on a quarterly basis. The evaluation ensures that supervisees are making progress in their clinical roles and are adhering to the organizational and ethical standards of practice.

Clinical Skills Development (20 points)

Evaluates the supervisee’s application of clinical knowledge and skills, case conceptualization, treatment planning, and therapeutic interventions.

Excellent (17-20 points):Demonstrates a comprehensive understanding of clinical concepts, consistently applies interventions appropriately, and creates effective treatment plans.
Proficient (13-16 points):Has a good understanding of clinical concepts, applies interventions correctly in most cases, and develops effective treatment plans with occasional guidance.
Needs Improvement (9-12 points):Shows some understanding of clinical concepts but struggles with consistently applying interventions. Requires frequent guidance for treatment planning.
Unsatisfactory (0-8 points):Lacks sufficient understanding of clinical concepts, frequently misapplies interventions, and requires constant supervision for treatment planning.

Professional Behaviors and Conduct (15 points)

Assesses the supervisee’s professionalism, punctuality, communication, and adherence to the organization’s code of conduct.

Excellent (13-15 points):Consistently demonstrates high levels of professionalism, maintains punctuality, communicates effectively, and adheres to organizational standards.
Proficient (10-12 points):Generally professional, with occasional lapses in punctuality or communication, but adheres to most organizational standards.
Needs Improvement (6-9 points):Shows inconsistencies in professional behavior, may struggle with punctuality or communication, and requires reminders about organizational standards.
Unsatisfactory (0-5 points):Demonstrates poor professionalism, frequently late, and struggles to adhere to basic conduct and communication standards.

Ethical and Legal Considerations (15 points)

Assesses the supervisee’s adherence to ethical guidelines, handling of confidentiality, and legal standards in clinical practice.

Excellent (13-15 points):Exemplary adherence to ethical standards, confidentiality is always maintained, and legal regulations are followed without issue.
Proficient (10-12 points):Follows ethical guidelines and maintains confidentiality in most cases, with minor lapses that are addressed quickly.
Needs Improvement (6-9 points):Some ethical or legal concerns have arisen, and supervisee requires guidance to ensure adherence.
Unsatisfactory (0-5 points):Significant ethical or legal violations have occurred, requiring corrective action or closer supervision.

Cultural Competency (10 points)

Evaluates the supervisee’s understanding of and sensitivity to cultural differences in the therapeutic process.

Excellent (9-10 points):Shows exceptional awareness and integration of cultural considerations in therapy, ensuring client-centered care.
Proficient (7-8 points):Understands cultural differences and applies cultural competence in most therapeutic settings.
Needs Improvement (4-6 points):Has basic cultural awareness but struggles to integrate cultural considerations consistently in practice.
Unsatisfactory (0-3 points):Lacks sufficient cultural competency, fails to consider cultural aspects in treatment planning.

Evidence-Based Practices (15 points)

Evaluates the supervisee’s ability to apply evidence-based practices and therapeutic interventions in their work with clients.

Excellent (13-15 points):Consistently applies evidence-based practices, staying updated on the latest interventions, and uses them effectively in client care.
Proficient (10-12 points):Applies evidence-based practices in most cases and demonstrates a working knowledge of current interventions.
Needs Improvement (6-9 points):Struggles to consistently apply evidence-based practices, requiring guidance on proper implementation.
Unsatisfactory (0-5 points):Rarely applies evidence-based practices, lacks understanding of current interventions.

Client Safety and Crisis Management (15 points)

Assesses the supervisee’s ability to manage client safety, respond to crises, and implement appropriate interventions for clients in distress.

Excellent (13-15 points):Proactively ensures client safety, demonstrates strong crisis management skills, and uses appropriate interventions in urgent situations.
Proficient (10-12 points):Responds effectively to most crises and manages client safety with occasional supervision.
Needs Improvement (6-9 points):Struggles with crisis management, occasionally requiring significant guidance to handle client safety issues.
Unsatisfactory (0-5 points):Demonstrates poor crisis management, frequently fails to ensure client safety, and requires constant supervision.

Documentation and Compliance (10 points)

Assesses the supervisee’s ability to maintain accurate and timely documentation in accordance with legal and organizational standards.

Excellent (9-10 points):Always maintains accurate, thorough, and timely documentation with minimal to no errors.
Proficient (7-8 points):Generally maintains accurate documentation but may occasionally need to correct minor errors or delays.
Needs Improvement (4-6 points):Documentation is inconsistent, with errors or delays that require regular correction.
Unsatisfactory (0-3 points):Frequently fails to maintain accurate or timely documentation, requiring significant intervention.

Total Points:

100 Points Possible

  • 90-100 Points: Excellent performance, exceeding expectations.
  • 75-89 Points: Proficient, meeting expectations.
  • 50-74 Points: Needs improvement, some areas require attention.
  • Below 50 Points: Unsatisfactory, performance must improve.
